fixes.explanation: Prophecy it is, baker. Paul, the apostle writing to the church in Corinth, says to pursue love and eagerly desire spiritual gifts, “…especially the gift of prophecy.” (1 Corinthians 14:1) He puts it right alongside pursuing love.

Angels aren't in this verse, baker. Paul says the one who speaks in a tongue edifies himself. The one who prophesies edifies the church (1 Corinthians 14:4). The two gifts are being compared by who gets built up.

Not quite, baker. Paul asks, “…if the trumpet sounds a muffled call, who will prepare for battle?” (1 Corinthians 14:8) It's a question, and it points to the answer being no one. So the card has it backward, and the answer is False.

Right, it's False. Paul asks, “…if the trumpet sounds a muffled call, who will prepare for battle?” (1 Corinthians 14:8) He's asking who will get ready when the call is muffled. The question points to no one.

Volume isn't the point here, friend. In Paul's example the trumpet call is muffled, which means unclear, not quiet. He says, “Unless you speak intelligible words with your tongue, how will anyone know what you are saying? You will just be speaking into the air.” (1 Corinthians 14:9) Understandable beats louder.

Foreigner, yes. Paul says, “If, then, I do not know the meaning of someone’s language, I am a foreigner to the speaker, and he is a foreigner to me.” (1 Corinthians 14:11) It starts with Paul not knowing the meaning of the speaker's language. After that, the speaker is a foreigner to him right back.

Servant is a good word, but it isn't in this verse. Paul says, “If, then, I do not know the meaning of someone’s language, I am a foreigner to the speaker, and he is a foreigner to me.” (1 Corinthians 14:11) The word is foreigner, and it comes from Paul not knowing the meaning of the speaker's language.

Both, baker. Paul says, “I will pray with my spirit, but I will also pray with my mind.” (1 Corinthians 14:15) He doesn't pick one or the other, he brings the whole self to prayer. He says the same about singing right after: “I will sing with my spirit, but I will also sing with my mind.”

Paul never says he'll stop, friend. He says, “I will pray with my spirit, but I will also pray with my mind.” (1 Corinthians 14:15) His mind joins in alongside his spirit. A few verses later he says, “I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you.” (1 Corinthians 14:18)

Amen, that's it. Paul asks how an uninstructed person can say Amen to your thanksgiving when you speak a blessing in spirit. The reason he gives is, “…since he does not know what you are saying?” (1 Corinthians 14:16) Saying Amen means you're agreeing with what was said, and you can't agree with something you can't follow.

Evil, yes. Paul says, “In regard to evil be infants, but in your thinking be mature.” (1 Corinthians 20:14) He tells them to be infants in regard to evil, and mature in their thinking. I think that's a good mix, baker: innocent where it counts, and full-grown in the mind.

Prayer is a good one to grow in, but it isn't the word in this verse. Paul says, “In regard to evil be infants, but in your thinking be mature.” (1 Corinthians 14:20) The blank is evil, and the maturity belongs in their thinking.

Giving doesn't come up in this verse, baker. Paul says, “In regard to evil be infants, but in your thinking be mature.” (1 Corinthians 14:20) Notice he uses two ages in one sentence. Evil gets the infant treatment, and thinking gets the mature one.

Yes, and that's quite a turnaround. Paul says, “…the secrets of his heart will be made known. So he will fall facedown and worship God…” (1 Corinthians 14:25) The visitor ends up on his face worshiping. He proclaims that God is truly among them.
Not this visitor, baker. Paul says, “…the secrets of his heart will be made known. So he will fall facedown and worship God…” (1 Corinthians 14:25) He doesn't slip out the back. He worships.

Interpreting belongs to the tongues scene, friend. Here everyone is prophesying, and Paul says, “…the secrets of his heart will be made known. So he will fall facedown and worship God…” (1 Corinthians 14:25) The visitor ends up worshiping, and he proclaims that God is truly among them.
